component_records.title: Program design, curriculum and track architecture
component_records.description: We deliver a single program design covering both tracks: Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) for low-income matriculating undergraduates and Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs) for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment, each with its own curriculum, schedule and outcome pathway, satisfying the requirement to develop the curriculum for and administer AI Prep. The curriculum is industry-informed, built with input from AI researchers and employer partners, and delivered as online AI courses with mentorship and real-world machine learning projects. Track A is structured around an academic-year and summer calendar aligned to employer internship hiring cycles, and Track B is delivered as an accelerated bootcamp-style alternative to a traditional degree, available part-time or full-time. The design also states the credentials awarded on completion, the training duration and cohort size, and the skill-attainment metrics used during training.

component_records.title: Outreach, recruitment and intake
component_records.description: We deliver a targeted outreach and recruitment strategy for low-income students and for unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented New Yorkers, run through community-based organizations, public and private colleges and universities across New York, and workforce partners. A single application and evaluation process screens applicants for both tracks, with a documented low-income eligibility definition and verification method, and a needs assessment at intake that identifies each participant's barriers to success (childcare, transportation, device and connectivity access, work schedule) and assigns the supports that address them. Recruitment targets are set to exceed the 250-participant minimum and to compete for the priority given to proposals serving more than 400 participants, with over 50% of participants low-income.

component_records.title: Training delivery, stipends and wrap-around supports
component_records.description: We deliver and manage the AI training program for both tracks, with instructors, teaching assistants and cohort managers running scheduled online sessions, labs and project work. Every participant receives a stipend at the proposed level plus wrap-around supports: an assigned industry mentor, a career coach with AI industry expertise, and success-coach check-ins for Track B participants. Professional development support runs throughout training — interview practice, portfolio and GitHub review, resume and LinkedIn coaching, and networking with employer partners — and skill-attainment is measured at defined checkpoints so progress can be evidenced to ESD. Stipend levels, participant counts and support costs are sized to fit within the $2M per track cap.

component_records.title: Employer partnerships, internships and job placement
component_records.description: We deliver an employer-relations function that cultivates and maintains relationships with leading New York technology employers, both to inform curriculum content and to generate paid internship and full-time openings. For Track A we place students in paid internships at leading New York tech companies, tailored to their skills and to employer hiring cycles, with internships designed as real-world project work that leads to full-time offers. For Track B we provide full-time job connection support in AI and closely related fields, including employer matching, referrals and post-placement follow-up. Placement activity is tracked against the target that the majority of graduates secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field, and we build the direct education-to-industry pathway and talent pipeline for AI employers that ESD is seeking.

component_records.title: Performance measurement and ESD reporting
component_records.description: We deliver a participant data system and reporting routine that tracks and records all information relevant to grant success and makes it available to ESD on request. The system captures, at minimum: applicant counts and the percentage who are low-income; enrollee counts and the percentage who are low-income; completer counts and the percentage who are low-income; paid internship placement rate and the percentage of placements that are low-income students; full-time job placement rate and the percentage of placements that are low-income individuals; participating colleges and universities; and participating employer partners. We produce the annual performance estimates against total participants served, low-income completion percentage and placement rate, justified from our historical program data and partner commitments, and we reconcile the data-point list with ESD at contract negotiation so the reporting scope is fixed early.

component_records.title: Budget, pricing and cost governance
component_records.description: We deliver a line-by-line budget mapped to the 18-month program duration and split by track, within the $2M per track and $4M both-track caps, with a written justification for every line. The budget is built on the three required cost categories: staff salary and benefits; wraparound supports and the proposed participant stipend level; and other program costs including curriculum development and implementation, marketing and events. Indirect costs are excluded entirely, and any cost match we offer is shown in ESD's budget template so it can be credited in scoring. The price proposal breaks out Personnel Services by job title, named employee where known, hourly or annual rate, fringe rate, percentage of time and cost to contract, and lists each Other Than Personnel Services cost on its own line with quantity and cost to contract. items.text: The RFP is issued by Empire State Development (ESD), a New York State economic development corporation whose mission is to promote a growing state economy, encourage business investment and job creation, and support diverse local economies through loans, grants, tax credits, real estate development and marketing.

ESD's Office of Strategic Workforce Development (OSWD) was created as part of a $350 million workforce development investment announced by Governor Kathy Hochul in April 2022, and is charged with aligning workforce programs to employer needs and creating opportunities for unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented workers.

ESD identifies AI as a high-growth sector advancing across healthcare, finance, transportation and manufacturing, and positions New York as an AI hub anchored by institutions such as Cornell Tech and state-backed initiatives such as Empire AI.

ESD's stated pain point is that rapid AI advancement may widen economic inequality, because many well-paying AI jobs require specialized education and technical training that low-income New Yorkers cannot access.

The program responds to tech recruiting practices that favor students at elite schools and candidates with personal connections to prominent technology companies, which AI Prep is intended to counter by training low-income New Yorkers in AI skills.
ESD currently has no AI Prep program administrator in place; it is procuring up to two qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum for and administer the program.

ESD wants up to two qualified program administrators to design the curriculum for and deliver AI Prep, an applied AI training program with two tracks: Track A "AI Prep 4 Internships" for low-income matriculating undergraduates and Track B "AI Prep 4 Jobs" for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment.

Track A deliverables are outreach and recruitment of low-income students, an application and evaluation process, needs assessments, industry-informed online AI curriculum with mentorship and real-world machine learning projects, participant stipends and wrap-around supports (mentors, career coaches), and placement of students in paid internships at leading New York tech companies leading to full-time jobs.

Track B deliverables are outreach to unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented New Yorkers, online AI courses built with industry input, an application and assessment process, part-time or full-time immersive training, stipends and success-coach supports, skill-attainment metrics, professional development, credentials where applicable, and full-time AI job placement support.
Both tracks require the administrator to cultivate and maintain relationships with leading industry employers to inform curriculum and generate paid internships or full-time jobs.
ESD will fund up to an 18-month operating period per selected administrator, with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need and availability of funds.
The anticipated contract start date is January 1, 2026, with award announced November 14, 2025.
The program must serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority for applicants proposing to serve more than 400.

Proposals are scored out of a maximum of 100 points by an ESD selection committee across Firm Qualifications (15), Experience (25), Project Plan (30), Cost of Services (20) and Diversity Practices (10).
Outcome targets are that over 50% of participants be low-income and that the majority of graduates secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.

Proposers must estimate annual performance against three metrics with justification from historical experience or partner commitments: total participants served annually, percentage of low-income participants completing the curriculum, and paid internship or full-time job placement rate of graduates.

Awarded administrators must track and report data including applicant and enrollee counts and low-income percentages, completion rates, internship and job placement rates, participating colleges and employers, with the exact data list set at contract negotiation.

Questions must be submitted by email to AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov by August 29, 2025, with ESD responses posted by September 12, 2025, and proposals are due by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025, with late proposals not accepted.
Interviews, if necessary, are scheduled for the first week of November 2025, and ESD reserves the right to change any date in the schedule.
ESD may conduct reference checks at its sole discretion on quality of services, ability to perform, and responsiveness, and may use that information in evaluation.

Budgets are capped at $2M per track and $4M for both tracks over the total contract period, with ESD investing up to $4M total to train and provide stipends for participants; proposals exceeding these amounts will not be considered.

Indirect costs are not an allowable expense, and budgets must map to Staff Salary and Benefits, Wraparound Supports and Participant Stipend Level, and other program costs such as curriculum development, marketing and events.
There is no cost-match requirement, but cost-matching earns additional points in scoring and must be shown in the budget template.

Applicants must be non-profit or for-profit entities with experience in at least three of four domains: academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training programs, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market; teams are allowed but one organization must be the lead.

Proposals must be submitted only as a two-part Technical and Administrative Proposal in a Dropbox folder named "company name – RFP title – date of Submission" via https://www.dropbox.com/request/AIPrep; fax, hardcopy and email submissions are not accepted.

The Technical Proposal must follow a fixed bookmark structure (cover page, table of contents, firm experience and qualifications, staff experience and qualifications, project plan and approach, cost of services, diversity practices questionnaire) and include no information beyond what is requested.

The Administrative Proposal must include, in order, the Non-Collusive Bidding Certification, Conflict of Interest Attestation, State Finance Law §§139-j/139-k forms, Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire, Iran Divestment Act Statement, EO-16 and EO-177 certifications, OCSD-1/OCSD-2/OCSD-4 diversity forms, NYS Businesses form, ST-220-CA or affidavit, and W-9; failure to submit any may result in rejection.

The contract carries a 30% MWBE participation goal and a 6% SDVOB participation goal, with Utilization Plans (OCSD-4) required at proposal stage and quarterly MWBE compliance reports and monthly SDVOB compliance reports (OCSD-6) during the term.

The selected contractor must carry Commercial General Liability of $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate, Commercial Auto of $1M, Sexual Abuse and Molestation insurance of $1M, and statutory Workers' Compensation and Disability coverage, naming ESD as additional insured with a waiver of subrogation.

Appendix A "ESD IT Security Standard Brief" and Appendix B "Diversity Practices Questionnaire" are referenced but their content is not included in the RFP text provided, so bidders must obtain them separately.

A sample Schedule A of standard ESD contract terms is referenced by link but not included; respondents must review it and submit any concerns in writing with the Administrative Proposal or waive objections.

A restricted period under the Procurement Lobbying Law runs until contract approval, barring contact about this procurement with any New York State employee other than designated contacts Julia Borukhov and Jordan Kaplan at AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov.
ESD has no AI Prep program administrator in place and is procuring up to two administrators to develop the curriculum and administer the program.
ESD gives priority to applicants proposing to serve more than 400 participants, against a stated minimum of 250.
The $2M per track cap covers both training and participant stipends.
ESD's outcome target is that the majority of graduates secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.
The exact data list is set at contract negotiation, so the reporting scope is not fully fixed at proposal stage.
Indirect costs are not an allowable expense under this grant.
The restricted period bars contact about this procurement with any New York State employee other than the designated contacts until contract approval.
The contract carries a 30% MWBE participation goal and a 6% SDVOB participation goal.
Applicants must have experience in at least three of four listed domains, and teams are allowed with one organization as lead.
The anticipated contract start date is January 1, 2026, with award announced November 14, 2025.
ESD will fund up to an 18-month operating period per administrator, with possible renewal or extension.
The bid is submitted as a single lead organization proposing both tracks under one integrated program office, on the reading that a combined-track bid is permitted and that the $4M cap then applies.

Low-income eligibility is defined as Pell Grant eligibility for Track A and as household income at or below 200% of the federal poverty level for Track B, with documentation collected at intake, pending ESD's confirmation of its own definition.
The 250-participant figure is treated as a floor and the proposal is sized above 400 participants to compete for the stated priority.
The 18-month term is priced as the full contract period, with the $2M per track cap applying across that same period and no revenue assumed beyond it.
Stipends are paid to participants from the ESD award and count against the per-track cap, at a level and count we propose in the budget.
Placement outcomes are measured within six months of program completion, using employer confirmation or offer letters as verification, until ESD fixes a window and method.
The reporting data set is assumed to be the minimum list in the RFP plus a small number of negotiated additions, and the reporting system is built to that list rather than to an open-ended scope.
The 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB goals are treated as commitments we must meet or document good faith efforts against, with Utilization Plans submitted at proposal stage and compliance reports thereafter.

Sexual Abuse and Molestation and Commercial Automobile coverages are carried even though the RFP qualifies the insurance list as applicable, because participants will be placed with third-party employers.

The Appendix A IT Security Standard Brief is assumed to require standard state-compliant hosting, access control and data protection for participant records, and the platform is configured to that baseline.

Schedule A concerns are submitted as a short written cover memo with the Administrative Proposal, separate from the Technical Proposal, to satisfy both the no-extra-information rule and the concerns requirement.
The Diversity Practices Questionnaire is obtained from ESD as a separate form and completed as its own Technical Proposal section.

Schedule A terms unseen but binding, and concerns must be filed blind. Schedule A, the standard ESD contract terms the successful respondent must accept, is referenced by link but not included in the RFP. The bidder must either submit written concerns with the Administrative Proposal or waive objections, without having read the terms it is objecting to; if Schedule A later contains unacceptable clauses (indemnity, IP, termination, audit), the bidder is bound or must negotiate after award, delaying the January 1, 2026 start. The RFP also forbids putting Schedule A information in the proposal while requiring concerns to accompany it, so the bidder risks a non-responsive submission either way. Schedule A is missing from the RFP and the RFP makes acceptance of it a contract condition (R265, R114) while requiring concerns to be filed with the Administrative Proposal (R264) and forbidding Schedule A content in the submission (R263). The conflict between R263 and R264 makes a compliant submission hard to construct.

Appendix A IT Security Standard Brief missing, so security scope and cost are unpriced. Appendix A, the ESD IT Security Standard Brief, is listed but not included, so the bidder cannot know the hosting, access-control, encryption, incident-reporting and audit obligations that will attach to the participant data platform. If the standard is stricter than assumed (for example State data-centre hosting, penetration testing or SOC 2 evidence), the platform configuration and compliance work are unplanned cost inside a capped budget, and a late discovery could delay go-live past the January 2026 start. The proposed solution explicitly assumes a 'standard state-compliant hosting, access control and data protection' baseline for Appendix A, which is an inference rather than a reading of the document. Security standards for State-funded programs commonly exceed that baseline, and the cost falls inside the $2M per track cap.

Combined-track bid may not be permitted, putting the $4M scope at risk. The RFP says ESD will award to up to two program administrators for Track A and/or Track B but does not say whether one bidder may hold both tracks. The proposed solution bids both tracks as a single lead organization on the reading that this is allowed and that the $4M cap then applies; if ESD instead treats the tracks as separate awards, the bid may be non-responsive or scored as a single-track proposal, and the integrated program office and shared platform economics no longer hold. The solution's first stated assumption is that a combined-track bid is permitted, and the RFP does not settle it. The whole pricing and staffing model depends on the $4M both-track cap.

Stipend level and participant count must be self-set inside a fixed cap. The $2M per track cap covers both training and participant stipends, but the RFP sets no stipend amount, no participant count above the 250 floor, and no rule on whether stipends count against the cap. The proposed solution sizes stipends and participant numbers itself while also targeting more than 400 participants to compete for priority; if the arithmetic is wrong or ESD expects a higher stipend, the bidder either over-commits and runs a deficit or under-bids and loses points on participant volume. The solution states stipends are paid from the award and count against the per-track cap, and that it will size above 400 participants, both as inferences. The RFP leaves stipend level, count and cap treatment open, so the cost model rests on assumptions the bidder alone controls.

Placement outcome target depends on employer partners the bidder does not yet control. The RFP expects the majority of graduates to secure paid internships or full-time AI employment, and requires employer commitment letters with the proposal, but the placement window and verification method are undefined. The proposed solution commits to that target and to placement tracking within six months of completion as an assumption; if employer hiring slows or ESD measures placement on a different basis, the bidder misses a scored outcome and risks the renewal case built on that data. The outcome target is a stated success criterion and the solution's renewal strategy rests on it, while the measurement window and method are unsettled. Placement depends on third-party employers whose commitments are not yet secured.

MWBE and SDVOB goals carry liquidated damages and material-breach exposure. The contract sets a 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB participation goal, with liquidated damages equal to the shortfall for willful MWBE failure and material breach for failing to use SDVOBs as planned, plus quarterly and monthly compliance reporting. The proposed solution commits to both goals and to the full reporting cadence; if certified firms cannot be found for the AI training scope or a named firm drops out, the bidder faces payment withholding, damages or a non-responsibility finding. The goals and remedies are explicit in the RFP, and the AI training and placement scope may have limited certified MWBE and SDVOB suppliers, which is an assumption rather than a known fact. The solution treats the goals as commitments to meet or document good faith against.

Administrative Proposal depends on many separately linked forms, any one of which can sink the bid. The Administrative Proposal must contain, in a fixed order, the Non-Collusive Bidding Certification, Conflict of Interest Attestation, 139-j/139-k forms, Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire and receipt, Iran Divestment Act Statement, EO-16 and EO-177 certifications, OCSD-1/2/4 forms, NYS Businesses form, ST-220-CA and W-9, and failure to submit any may result in rejection. All of these are separate linked documents or external systems, and the Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire must have been completed within one year of submission. A single missing or stale item, or a wrong questionnaire variant, can disqualify an otherwise strong bid. The RFP lists roughly a dozen separately sourced administrative items with rejection as the stated consequence, and the Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire carries a one-year currency condition. The proposed solution commits to all of them but the risk is in execution against external forms.

Appendix B Diversity Practices Questionnaire missing, worth 10 scoring points. The Diversity Practices Questionnaire is a required Technical Proposal section and carries 10 of the 100 evaluation points, but neither the form nor its content is in the RFP. A bidder that cannot obtain the form either omits a mandatory section, risking rejection, or submits a self-designed questionnaire that may not be scored as intended, losing up to a tenth of the score. The questionnaire is both a mandatory submission item (R101) and a scored section, and it is absent from the RFP text. The proposed solution assumes it will be obtained from ESD as a separate form, which is not confirmed.

Budget template and cost-match scoring rules not provided. The RFP says cost matching earns additional points and must be shown in ESD's budget template, but the template is not included and the points-per-match formula is not stated. The bidder cannot tell how much match is worth buying, so it either leaves points on the table or commits match it cannot fund, and a budget submitted in the wrong format may be treated as non-responsive. The budget template is a listed gap and the RFP states no cost-match requirement yet awards points for matching (R054), with no scoring formula given. Cost of Services is 20 of 100 points, so format and match presentation directly affect the score.

Low-income definition is self-defined and drives eligibility, targets and reporting. The RFP does not define 'low-income' or 'barriers to employment', yet the definition determines recruitment, the over-50% low-income target, stipend eligibility and the reporting data set. The proposed solution adopts Pell eligibility for Track A and 200% of the federal poverty level for Track B pending ESD confirmation; if ESD applies a different definition, intake screening, documentation and reported percentages must be rebuilt mid-program, and the low-income share may fall below target. The definition is undefined in the RFP and the solution's choice is an explicit inference. The low-income share is both a success criterion and a reported metric, so a mismatch has direct scoring and compliance consequences.

Reporting scope is fixed only at contract negotiation. The RFP requires tracking of a minimum data list but leaves the exact data points, frequency and format to contract negotiation. The proposed solution builds the reporting system to the minimum list plus a few negotiated additions; if ESD adds fields, systems or cadence after award, the participant data system needs rework and the reporting effort is unpriced inside the cap. The solution states the reporting scope is not fixed at proposal stage and prices to the minimum list. Reporting is a mandatory obligation with an open-ended data list, so scope growth is plausible rather than exceptional.

Eighteen-month term may be too short to deliver internships and placements for the first cohort. The contract runs up to 18 months from January 1, 2026, and the proposal must show a monthly timeline through completion of internships or full-time jobs for the first cohort. The proposed solution spends months 1–3 on curriculum build and months 2–5 on recruitment, leaving roughly a year for delivery and placement; if recruitment slips or employer hiring cycles do not align, the first cohort's placements fall outside the term and the outcome data ESD scores and renews on is incomplete. The solution prices the 18-month term as the full contract period with no revenue beyond it, and front-loads three months of build before any delivery. The RFP leaves renewal terms open, so a slip cannot be recovered by extension with certainty.

Technical Proposal content limits conflict, risking a non-responsive submission. The RFP requires the Technical Proposal to provide all requested information clearly and completely while also forbidding any information beyond what is specifically requested, and separately requires Schedule A concerns to be filed with the Administrative Proposal while barring Schedule A content from the submission. The proposed solution handles this with a separate cover memo, but a reviewer applying the strict rule could still treat narrative, marketing material or the concerns memo as excess content and mark the proposal non-responsive. Two pairs of requirements pull in opposite directions (R102 against R113, and R263 against R264), and the RFP makes following instructions a mandatory requirement. The solution's workaround is an inference, not a confirmed reading.
